clarifyingQuestions: Does updating an existing key count as an access?
How should ties be broken among keys with the same frequency?
Are expired entries removed lazily or by background cleanup?
followUps: Make `get` and `put` O(1) when TTL cleanup is disabled.
Add hit/miss/eviction metrics split by TTL and capacity evictions.
Add thread safety around buckets and entries.
followUpGuide: For O(1) LFU without TTL cleanup, keep `key -> entry`, `freq -> OrderedDict`, and `min_freq`. Moving a key means deleting it from the old bucket, incrementing frequency, and appending it to the new bucket.
With TTL, decide whether cleanup can be lazy and opportunistic or needs a separate min-heap by expiry time. Lazy cleanup is simpler but can scan many expired entries during `put`.
For metrics, count expired `get` as a miss and a TTL eviction. Count capacity eviction only after expired entries are cleaned.
For thread safety, use one `threading.RLock` around all entry and bucket mutations. `get` is a write because it increments frequency and changes recency.
complexityAnalysis: - Naive LFU approach: scan all keys to find the lowest frequency on eviction. Time: O(n) per eviction. Space: O(n).
- Frequency buckets approach: map keys to nodes and frequencies to ordered buckets. Time: O(1) average get/set/evict for pure LFU ops. Space: O(n).

- TTL-aware LFU (shipped guide): live hits and live-key updates use O(1) average dictionary/bucket operations, treating key hashing and comparisons as constant work. A new-key put scans n entries and recomputes the minimum over b occupied frequency buckets, so it costs O(n) and uses O(n) temporary list space. An expired get or immediately expired put recomputes that minimum in O(b), which can be O(n). Persistent metadata is O(n), apart from stored values and key sizes.

- An expiry heap gives O(log h) insertion/removal per heap event, where h includes stale deadlines left by updates. Validate each popped deadline against the current entry and bound stale heap growth. A separate ordered frequency structure is still needed if arbitrary expiry must preserve efficient minimum-frequency lookup.
solutionGuide: Keep three pieces of state: a key-to-entry map, a frequency-to-ordered-keys map, and `min_freq`. Each bucket is ordered by recency, so the first key in the lowest-frequency bucket is the eviction victim.

On `get`, reject expired entries before touching frequency. On `put`, a non-positive TTL removes only that key. Otherwise update a live existing key as an access, or clean expired entries before admitting a new key and evicting from the `min_freq` bucket if needed. Read the injected clock once per operation so all those decisions use the same timestamp.
